Solution

d OurBigBook.com
Take r>0 and select a complex argument θ for z. To specify the complex exponentiation, use z1+i=exp((1+i)(lnr+iθ)). Expanding its exponent gives
z1+i=elnr−θei(θ+lnr).
(26)
Its complex logarithm therefore has values
ℜf=lnr−θ,ℑf=θ+lnr+2πk,k∈Z.​
(27)
The continuous logarithm obtained by retaining the displayed exponent uses k=0. If the outer logarithm is the principal logarithm, choose k to put the imaginary part in (−π,π] instead; the real part is unchanged. In particular one cannot generally assert Log(ew)=w without checking its imaginary part.
The condition on the real part gives lnr=θ, so the required logarithmic spiral has polar coordinates
r=eθ,z(θ)=eθ(cosθ+isinθ).​
(28)
As θ increases, it runs from the negative real axis near radius e−π through −ie−π/2, 1 and ieπ/2 to the negative real axis at radius eπ. The angle increases by one complete turn. Using the conventional principal argument −π<θ≤π, the inner negative-axis endpoint is excluded and the outer endpoint is included. The convention −π≤θ<π reverses those endpoint choices. If both limiting arguments are admitted by the paper's wording, both limiting endpoints are drawn; the interior curve is the same. The origin is never included because the complex logarithm is undefined there.

V=2π∫0R​rRe−r/Rdr=2πR3∫01​ue−udu.

Here u=r/R. Using integration by parts, ∫01​ue−udu=[−(u+1)e−u]01​=1−2/e. Hence
R=[2π(1−2/e)V​]1/3.​

A(z)=4LbHz​​(2−Hz​).
(31)
The volume integral, followed by integration by substitution u=z/H, is
Vbank​​=∫0H​A(z)dz=4LbH∫01​(2u1/2−u3/2)du=4LbH(34​−52​)=1556​LbH.​​

In the x,z plane, the embankment lies above the parabola z=Hx2/L2 and below z=H. The bore has circular cross-section
D={(x,z):x2+(z−D/2)2≤D2/4}.
(33)
It touches the valley floor at the origin. To check that this entire disk lies inside the projected embankment, its equation gives x2≤Dz−z2≤Dz. Since HD/L2<1, it follows that Hx2/L2≤z, with strict inequality away from the bottom contact. Also z≤D<H. Thus no circular segment needs to be subtracted from the tunnel section.
For each (x,z) in the disk, the length of bore inside the material is the local width 2b(2−z/H). The required volume integral is therefore
Vcut​=∬D​2b(2−Hz​)dxdz.
(34)
The disk has area A=πD2/4 and centroid height D/2, so ∬D​zdxdz=AD/2. Applying the volume of a solid with affine thickness formula gives
Vcut​=2bA(2−2HD​)=πbD2(1−4HD​).​
(35)
The width varies along the circular section; multiplying its area by the top width alone would miss this variation.

Let M=2x+ey and N=xey−cosy. Their cross partial derivatives agree: My​=ey=Nx​. On the simply connected plane, this makes the differential form exact. Integrating Fx​=M gives F=x2+xey+h(y); matching Fy​=N then requires h′(y)=−cosy, so one potential is
F(x,y)=x2+xey−siny.
(36)
The ordinary differential equation states dF/dx=0 along a solution. Its initial condition fixes the constant to F(1,π/2)=eπ/2. Hence the solution is specified implicitly by
x2+xey−siny=eπ/2,y(1)=2π​.​
(37)
At the initial point Fy​=eπ/2=0, so the implicit function theorem guarantees a unique local branch y(x) through that point.

Work on an open domain with xy>0 and x=0, where the displayed square root is real and differentiable. Split u=v+h with v=ϕ(xy) and h=xy​ψ(y/x). For the first term, the chain rule gives
vxx​=y2ϕ′′(xy),vyy​=x2ϕ′′(xy),
(49)
so x2vxx​−y2vyy​=0.
For the second term, set t=y/x. Its first partial derivatives are
hx​=xxy​​(21​ψ(t)−tψ′(t)),hy​=yxy​​(21​ψ(t)+tψ′(t)).
(50)
They show xhx​+yhy​=h, the degree-one case of Euler theorem for homogeneous functions. Differentiating that identity with respect to each variable yields
xhxx​+yhxy​=0,xhxy​+yhyy​=0.
(51)
The mixed partial derivatives agree here by the chain rule. Multiplying these equations by x and y, respectively, proves the second derivative identity for a degree-one homogeneous function:
x2hxx​=−xyhxy​=y2hyy​.
(52)
Adding the results for v and h verifies the partial differential equation
x2uxx​−y2uyy​=0.​
(53)
Equivalently, h(λx,λy)=λh(x,y) for positive λ, so the same proof follows directly from its homogeneous function property. The statement is local to a domain where the given expression is defined; it does not require assigning values on x=0.

The finite form of Taylor's theorem is
f(x)=k=0∑n−1​k!f(k)(a)​(x−a)k+Rn​(x),Rn​(x)=n!f(n)(ξ)​(x−a)n,​
(54)
where ξ lies between a and x when x=a. Sufficient hypotheses are continuous derivatives up to order n−1 on the interval joining the endpoints and an nth derivative in its interior. The first n terms end at degree n−1; the Taylor remainder uses the nth derivative. At x=a the remainder is zero. This finite Taylor polynomial identity does not require convergence of an infinite Taylor series.

a OurBigBook.com
Use the intended model of uniform draws and a replacement decision independent of the first ball's colour, with probability r. The marginal specification P(R)=r alone would not determine the experiment if replacement depended on that colour. This independence assumption is used throughout the question.
Write Bj​ for a non-blue draw and R for no replacement. The sample space consists of the eight ordered outcomes obtained by choosing one of B1​,B1​, then one of R,R, then one of B2​,B2​. The chain rule for probabilities gives their probabilities:
outcomeB1​∩R∩B2​B1​∩R∩B2​B1​∩R∩B2​B1​∩R∩B2​B1​∩R∩B2​B1​∩R∩B2​B1​∩R∩B2​B1​∩R∩B2​​probability4r/256r/256r/259r/25(1−r)/103(1−r)/103(1−r)/103(1−r)/10​​​
(59)
For example, the first entry is (2/5)r(2/5). The fifth is (2/5)(1−r)(1/4) because one blue ball has been removed. With no replacement after a non-blue first draw, the two remaining colours each have two balls, explaining the last two entries. The first four entries sum to r and the last four to 1−r, so the full sample space has total probability one. At r=0 or 1, the corresponding impossible outcomes simply have zero probability.

Let C=B1​∩B2​. Under replacement its joint probability is

In the latter case the first removed ball is non-blue, so all NB​ blue balls remain. Applying Bayes' theorem and cancelling the positive common factors yields the posterior replacement probability after different-colour draws:
g(r)=P(R∣C)=r/N+(1−r)/(N−1)r/N​=N−rr(N−1)​.​

It does not depend on NB​. To prove the requested bound directly,
r−g(r)=N−rr(1−r)​≥0,0≤r≤1.​

Equality holds at r=0 and r=1, and the inequality is strict between them. Its sketch joins (0,0) to (1,1), stays below the diagonal, and is increasing and convex because

The interpretation is that removing a non-blue ball increases the chance of blue on the second draw; seeing the two different colours therefore favours the no-replacement explanation.
